newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia c.bank satisfied with current T-bill yields.
newsitem.headline: Russia c.bank satisfied with current T-bill yields.

text.p: The Russian central bank will not push falling Treasury bill yields even lower and is focusing on maintaining domestic investors' share of the market, chairman Sergei Dubinin said on Wednesday.

"We are not aiming to force a decrease in yields on the GKO (discount Treasury bill) market as there might be a forcing out of Russian investors, which we are not interested in," Dubinin told a news conference.
Yields have dropped sharply, with a 364-day T-bill averaging 20.00 percent at auction on Wednesday. Yields were close to 30 percent in early May.

But the central bank chairman said he was concerned about commercial banks, which made a healthy living from extremely high T-bill yields of around 200 percent a year ago, but could be damaged by a quick, sharp yields fall.

Dubinin said Russia would maintain a quota of 15 percent for foreign participants in the market, though other central bank officials said no official cap was in place. They said the bank's goal was to keep foreign holdings below 30 percent.
"The current quota (of non-resident participation) serves the interests of the Russian Federation and foreign investors and will remain at about the current level," Dubinin said.
Deputy bank chairman Andrei Kozlov, in charge of the T-bill markets, said foreigners held more than 20 percent of the paper.
The bank's director for Open Markets Operations, Konstantin Korishchenko, told Reuters that the bank had no quota system to stop foreign T-bill buying.

"Essentially, we are talking about what kind of share of the market we want foreign investors to have," he said. "Our goal is not to increase the non-resident share, but the central bank does not impose any quotas."
Dubinin said the bank also was not planning to lower its refinancing rate, which is effectively a cap on T-bill yields and is currently 24 percent.
But he said bank reserves had continued to skyrocket in June, continuing a half-year trend which has seen sharp demand for roubles to buy Treasury bills, as well as to pay taxes.
Russia's gross gold and currency reserves rose to $23.8 billion on July 1 from $20 billion on June 23.
Gold and currency reserves last year fell to $11.2 billion.

"By buying hard currency and gold, we are carrying out an emission," Dubinin said. "There has been a considerable increase in hard currency/gold reserves." But growth of reserves would probably slow in the second half of the year due to seasonal dollar sales, he said.
